stories.headline: Update: Trump Tells France to 'Close Your Borders' as About 1,800 Are Arrested in Violent Protests
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump on Sunday urged France to secure its borders as protests continued across the country, with police arresting approximately 1,800 people in violent demonstrations. In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote: "France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"

The new development is the president's direct intervention in the French crisis, which has seen buildings set ablaze and widespread property damage in Paris, Limoges and other cities. Coverage of his remarks has spread across more than 20 outlets. President Emmanuel Macron has acknowledged intelligence failures, and the unrest has triggered political fallout in Paris.

Supporters of the president's comments, including many conservative commentators, frame the unrest as the consequence of immigration and integration policies they say have failed. Critics, including many on the left and French officials, argue that the remarks inflame tensions and mischaracterize the causes of the protests. French authorities have not framed the demonstrations solely around immigration.

The arrests are expected to bring a wave of prosecutions in the coming days, while the French government faces pressure over how it handled security and intelligence ahead of the unrest.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Takes Up Challenge to Federal Ban on Home Distilling
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court announced Monday that it will hear a challenge to a 160-year-old federal law barring the distilling of alcohol at home. The court said in an orders list released Monday morning that it will take up Department of Justice v. Scott McNutt, with oral arguments to be scheduled later this term.

The justices had two pending cases over the ban and opted to take up the appeal brought by the federal government. The question before the court is whether the prohibition oversteps the federal government's constitutional powers. A ruling against the government could strike down the long-standing restriction.

The case touches on the scope of federal authority under the Constitution, an issue that has drawn interest from libertarian-leaning and conservative legal advocates who argue Congress lacks power to ban a private activity in the home. The Justice Department defends the law as a legitimate exercise of federal authority tied to alcohol taxation and regulation, and has pointed to revenue and public safety concerns.

A decision is expected by the end of the court's term, likely in the summer of 2027.

stories.headline: Musk Pledges One SpaceX Share to Every Child in America
stories.summary:
Elon Musk said Monday he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every "kid" in America next year. In a post on X shortly before 4 a.m. ET, he wrote: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."

At current stock prices, the pledge would amount to roughly an $11 billion giveaway, nearly double Michael Dell's record-breaking gift to Trump accounts. Musk did not specify whether "kid" means all minors under 18 or some other group, and gave no details on how the shares would be distributed or held.

The announcement came a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic said it will commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund ahead of its stock market listing, suggesting a growing trend of tech wealth being directed toward public-facing programs.

Many questions remain, including eligibility, tax treatment, custodianship and whether the offer connects to the federal Trump accounts program for children. Further details are expected from Musk or SpaceX.

stories.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines Critically Injured After Being Hit by Car in Apparent Deliberate Attack
stories.summary:
Independent Australian MP Helen Haines, 65, is in critical condition at a Melbourne hospital after being struck by a car outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, Victoria, on Monday afternoon. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident appeared to be a deliberate act, stating: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear." Counter-terror police are involved in the investigation.

Police say a white Toyota Landcruiser hit Haines at about 3:35 p.m. local time. A 43-year-old man from nearby Tarrawingee was subdued and held by passersby before being arrested, and police say a knife was found in the vehicle. Victoria Police are investigating whether the act was intentional and have said they do not believe there is an ongoing threat to the community. It is not yet known whether the suspect and Haines knew each other. Haines was first taken to a Wangaratta hospital and then flown to Melbourne by helicopter.

Albanese said it was too early to determine a motive but noted that the political temperature in Australia had been rising, saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy." Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke cited figures showing reports of threatening or harassing behavior toward politicians rose from 951 to 1,067 over the past year.

Haines, elected in 2019, is widely regarded across the political spectrum as an anti-corruption campaigner. She proposed legislation in 2021 for a national anti-corruption watchdog and is credited with helping drive creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, whose oversight committee she sits on. Leaders from across party lines have expressed shock and sent messages of support.

stories.headline: Update: Saudi Capital on Edge as Houthi Attacks Prompt Riyadh Skyscraper to Order Remote Work
stories.summary:
Escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels have rattled Riyadh, with management of the 99-story Kingdom Centre ordering all office employees to work remotely until further notice. The directive, first reported by Agence France-Presse, affects a landmark whose tenants include Merrill Lynch, McKinsey & Company and the International Monetary Fund. The shopping mall at the base of the tower remained open to the public.

The move followed a Saudi-led coalition announcement that it had intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area, a third over the Eastern Province and two ballistic missiles in southern Saudi Arabia overnight. Authorities had earlier issued a threat alert for the capital. Building management did not state a reason for the order, but it came amid repeated missile and drone attacks that have disrupted the city.

The development adds to a widening regional conflict tied to the Iran war, which has seen Houthi strikes on Saudi targets and Yemen's government palace. Fox News also reported that Iran has issued a new warning to the United States and that Qatar is preparing to announce a regional defense agreement, signaling Gulf states are moving to bolster their security as the conflict spreads. Further details of the Qatari arrangement have not been released.

stories.headline: Ex-OpenAI Engineer Accused of Planting Recording Device Had Saudi Government Support, Prosecutors Say
stories.summary:
US prosecutors allege that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national and former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly planting an audio recorder in an OpenAI meeting room, had "considerable support" from the Saudi government. A California court filing says he was in frequent communication with a member of the Saudi royal family. Prosecutors cited this in arguing he is a flight risk who should be detained pending trial.

OpenAI found the device on September 30, plugged into the back of a TV and covered with toilet paper. A camera installed in the room filmed Alfozan on October 5 looking behind the television. The FBI arrested him on October 9, and his contract was terminated. The filing says his arrest came three days before a scheduled one-way flight from San Francisco to Riyadh.

Prosecutors say his wife and son flew to Doha the day after the arrest on a one-way business class ticket paid for by a Saudi military official. The filing argues the conduct could endanger US national security because OpenAI executives met with government officials in the room while the device was believed to be installed. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan was scheduled to appear in federal court in San Francisco on Monday. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The FBI investigation is ongoing.

stories.headline: National Guard Member Shot in Leg While Trying to Break Up Street Fight in Washington
stories.summary:
A National Guard member was shot in the leg late Sunday while trying to intervene in a street fight in Washington, D.C., police said. Jeffery Carroll, interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, told reporters on Monday that one of the men involved in the fight pulled a gun and opened fire after the guard member stepped in to break it up.

The wounded service member was hit in the leg. The article text provided did not detail his condition, the identity of the shooter, or whether an arrest had been made, and those details were not immediately available.

The shooting drew coverage from 21 outlets across the political spectrum. National Guard troops have been deployed on the streets of the capital, and any attack on them is likely to renew debate over the deployment. Supporters of the presence argue it deters crime and protects residents, while critics question whether troops should be performing policing functions. Further details from police and the Guard are expected as the investigation proceeds.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Declines to Hear 9/11 Defendants' Appeal to Reinstate Plea Deals
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear appeals from three men accused of plotting the September 11, 2001, attacks who are awaiting trial at Guantanamo Bay. The justices turned away petitions from Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Attash without explanation.

The defendants had sought to hold the government to plea agreements reached with military prosecutors. Those deals would have shielded them from the death penalty, but the Biden administration revoked them. The refusal leaves the revocation in place and means the cases continue toward trial before the military commission, which has been delayed for years by pretrial litigation.

In other action Monday, the court said it will consider the constitutionality of a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on distilling spirits at home, after a lower court struck down restrictions dating to the 1860s. The Trump administration urged the justices to take that case. The court also agreed to hear a challenge to magnet school admissions policies in Montgomery County, Maryland, in a new test of educational diversity efforts and when such policies may be challenged as racially discriminatory.

stories.headline: Anthropic to Commit Share of Its Stock to a 'Public Benefit Fund' Ahead of Listing
stories.summary:
Anthropic, one of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies, said Sunday it plans to commit a small percentage of its stock to a new Public Benefit Fund. In a blog post titled "Investing in the public benefit," the company described a new entity with a structure that increases its stake as the company grows.

The announcement comes ahead of what BBC News described as a blockbuster stock market listing. Details such as the exact percentage, the fund's governance and how the money would be spent were not specified in the excerpted coverage.

The move was covered by six outlets, and BBC reported that Elon Musk made a related announcement in response. It reflects growing scrutiny of how AI developers share the wealth and influence they are accumulating, and it may shape expectations for other AI firms considering public offerings.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Warns U.S. Against Renewed Attack, Says It Has 'Unfinished Jobs' Too
stories.summary:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned Washington on Sunday against renewing attacks, saying Tehran has "unfinished jobs" of its own. In a post on X, he wrote: "Last time you wanted to 'finish the job,' Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too."

Araghchi also said Tehran's seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remains on the table, with conditions attached. Separately, the United States urged Americans across the Middle East to remain vigilant amid regional security concerns and possible travel disruptions.

The exchange comes as the Middle East war has widened in recent days, with Houthi strikes on Saudi targets. Vice President JD Vance has said the U.S. has "decisively won" the war in some ways, while Washington has reportedly weighed options against Iran's underground nuclear sites. The warning signals that Tehran does not consider the conflict settled.

stories.headline: Update: Mulvaney Predicts Wiles Will Leave After Midterms as White House Chief of Staff's Standing Questioned
stories.summary:
Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said Sunday that he expects current chief of staff Susie Wiles to leave her post after the midterm elections, though on her own terms. His comments followed reports suggesting she may have lost President Trump's confidence. Mulvaney said Wiles is in a "powerful place" for now. Trump told NBC News in a phone call that she would remain in her role, pointing to the success of the first two years of his second term.

The remarks came amid a week of turmoil at the White House, including the ouster of press secretary Katie Zacharia after five days and a bipartisan backlash over Trump's waiver of Russia sanctions and a diesel deal with Moscow. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that the deal did not amount to sanctions relief, while former Vice President Mike Pence called for sanctions to be restored. Zelensky told NBC that Ukraine trusts America but hopes Trump will "change his decisions."

Other developments included Trump's announcement of a plan by architect Tom Fazio to rebuild East Potomac Golf Links, with work to begin Nov. 15 despite a judge's order pausing changes until at least Oct. 26. Reports also said Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a summit with Trump and Xi Jinping next month on ending the Ukraine war. Former President Obama accused the administration of targeting Rep. Ilhan Omar, while administration officials have said investigators have a strong case.

An NBC News poll found the share of Americans who say the country is on the wrong track is the highest of Trump's second term. Democrats are campaigning on that mood ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, while Republicans point to their fundraising advantage and warn that poll enthusiasm may not translate into turnout.

stories.headline: Update: Grass Fire at Alberta Military Base Kills 4 Canadian Soldiers, Injures 39
stories.summary:
A grass fire at a Canadian military training area in Alberta killed four service members and injured 39 others, 19 of them critically, officials said. The fire swept through the area while soldiers were training with live ammunition. Canada's defense minister confirmed the casualty figures.

The cause of the fire remains unknown. Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the worst peacetime tragedies in the history of the Canadian military.

The new development is the confirmed death toll and the number of critically injured. An investigation into the cause is expected, and the condition of the critically wounded will determine whether the toll rises.

stories.headline: Update: France Faces Political Fallout After Nationwide Riots as Macron Acknowledges Intelligence Failures
stories.summary:
French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged "failures in anticipation and intelligence" after weekend unrest, while ruling out the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. Nunez conceded that police "lost control" during the protests. Around half a million people marched over poor school conditions and the cost of living, but the demonstrations were overshadowed by looting and arson that led to about 1,800 arrests nationwide.

Macron blamed "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," and promised a "hard line," saying those who looted would pay for the damage. In a televised address he also called for dialogue. The far left and far right have accused each other of stirring up the disorder, and the violence largely subsided on Sunday.

The unrest has raised alarm across Europe, where cost-of-living protests have also appeared in Italy, Belgium and Portugal and elections are due in at least half a dozen countries next year. Citi strategist Beata Manthey expects continued volatility in French equities until at least the summer because of political and fiscal uncertainty.

stories.headline: Update: Middle East War Widens as Houthi Strikes Hit Saudi Targets and Yemen's Government Palace
stories.summary:
The Iran-linked Houthis continued missile and drone attacks across the region. Yemen's information minister said ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace but that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said a Houthi attack caused a "limited fire" at Aramco's headquarters complex in Dhahran.

BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency found 12 vessels were struck in a week, and 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was hit by a projectile. Other reporting said around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped near the Strait of Hormuz. Experts say US military assistance and pipelines bypassing the strait have helped Gulf exports rebound.

Elsewhere, the UN agency for Palestinians said the number of people it helps will fall by about a third, from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. The BBC also reported masked settlers attacking Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank; the Israeli military condemned the violence, while the prime minister's office called the reports part of a "smear" campaign.
